projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ahnolia Gill was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: This is JANE PURTLE. I am in New Summerfield, Texas on July 13, 1995. I'm making this recording for the Cherokee County Historical Commission with AHNOLIA GILL. She was--her husband was in World War II and her son served in Vietnam. So we are going to be talking about--little bit about both of those wars and also, about some of the conditions that were present at the time of World War II. What sort of thing was happening in Cherokee County during World War II? Ahnolia, first I'm going to ask you just a little bit about your own background and if you don't mind telling me about when you were born. You don't have to tell me the exact--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, I don't mind.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Alright and where you were born.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: I was born about--it's about six miles of New Emmaus--and I was born May the 20th, 1921.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Okay and your parents were?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Allie and Ray Murphy.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Alright. I've made a recording with her brother, Rex Murphy about some other things so I feel like I have some connections with you.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --with you. You were married to Roscoe Gill.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Alright, just tell a little of that history so we'll know what his involvement was at the time that World War II started.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, he--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: You were married when?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: We married in January, January the 18th of 1941 and then he left for--he was drafted for this year's draft that they had back then in the first part of March. I don't know the exact date but it was the first part of March of 1941.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And he did his training where?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Edgewood Arsenal in Maryland.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And what kind of training was that?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Chemical Warfare. He was attached to the Air Force after he finished his basic training.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Why--tell about his education so we'll know a little bit about his background.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: He was--well he had a degree from A and M in Heart Culture.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And so whenever he was drafted they decided to put him in chemical warfare?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: I guess. Anyway that's where they sent you.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Okay, so you were going to be with him. Tell about your--did you go to Georgia or any place?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh (Answered affirmatively). He was trans--he was--when he finished his basic training in Maryland, well they sent him to Hunter field in Savannah, Georgia, and then I went to him. I couldn't --I couldn't go to Pennsylvania while he was in basic training, but, then I went to him in Savannah.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: By that time, had the war been declared?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yes. Well no. No it hadn't. Not at that time because that was--we married in January and he left in March but then he got out in October of 1941, and we came back to New Summerfield and started building our house. And then war--cause war the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor the 7th of December of 1941.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So he--he had already been discharged for that time?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Tell about why that happened.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well his daddy was almost blind and they had the--their uncle had died--great-uncle, had died and left all but he had four, there was four of the children. There was him and two sisters and a brother. And he couldn't--his--where we lived where our house was the--they had cows that was undivided--it was undivided interest at that time and so they--they let him out in October. Course, weren't expecting to be a war but we did.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Uh huh, right.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: And--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --Well now he--he was injured at one--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: At Macon. In Macon--that was in '40, the last part of '41 or '42, first part of '42 because he moved to Macon, Georgia from Savannah, Georgia and was given an emergency leave to bring me home because I was--I was pregnant with our first child.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And then he went back.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yes, he went back to Macon, Georgia. He just had an emergency leave and went back to Macon, Georgia and--and was playing volleyball and he was paralyzed for 15 days. They--he hurt himself some way. And it took--and for 15 days after he went--it was right after he went back, that he got hurt and--and then he would just got where he could kind of walk real good whenever our oldest child was born in February of '43. I guess. Yeah, I know he was.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So he never did go overseas?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, he didn't go overseas.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Would you say some things about what life was like in Cherokee County during World War II?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, it was--everything was rationed. You better take care of your tires and your gas. You didn't get very much. You better not have a car that used too much gas. And shoes were rationed. You had to have stamps to get shoes and when you got a baby, it's hard to make it with stamps because their feet don't stop growing just because you don't have a stamp.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Uh huh. What else do you remembered being rationed?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well I remembered, let's see, sugar was rationed. But I can't remember what else was. I slept a few nights since then.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Ah, meat. Did you have you have to have stamps for meat?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: I don't remember having--maybe it's because we had our own meat. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Do you remember what was hard to find to buy?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I can't. Not really. I'm not--mostly I just remember the tires and gasoline and shoes because I had such a time getting shoes for the baby, was rationed. You had to have a stamp to get the shoes.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Did you ever trade stamps with anybody?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yes, I--a lady up-- that run the store up here in Summerfield, Mrs. Elbridge, I believe was here name. She gave me her stamps. She said she wasn't buying shoes. She gave me her stamp to buy shoes for the baby and then when --of course when we got enough--when we got another book of stamps, well I carried her, her stamp back.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: How often did they issue stamps? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: But you did get a book and--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --they had to do a certain period of time--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --and then you would get another one?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)--get another one.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And did you get one for every member of the family, a book? Did you get one for the children?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well now I don't--I don't remember where--you know, I really and truly I don't remember where we--you know--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What about the way other people around the area, were a lot of the men being drafted into service?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively) There was a lot of them, we had a neighbor up here, they were twins and he was one of the Roy Wallace. And Ray Wallace was killed during and I think that was in World War II. But they were just more people gone, then more men gone then were around.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: How did life change? How did things change as a result of the war? I know you talked about how hard it was to get around.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, they was--it was--there was more money. We didn't--cause we just come out of the depression during the--you know, when the war, but --

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So you were able to buy more things?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: You could buy it but you couldn't buy it cause you didn't have stamps. You had more money but couldn't buy it because--because you didn't have stamps to buy with.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Can you think of any other effects--how--what about people on their church going? Was--did that effect--was that an effect of the war?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, we had our churches where I--I lived just a half a mile from New Summerfield and I--we got churches all around, you know, here.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So you could go walk--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: So --yes, you could if you had too. You could--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: But you just didn't get to go?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, oh no, you didn't waste gas to go driving. You couldn't waste much gas to go to Jacksonville, but you could coast down Mud Creek Hill but then you had to use your gas to go up on the other side.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So you really did watch the gas that much?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh, you did.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: You would gage how many gallons it took you to get to Jacksonville?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: and try to decide if you really had enough to --

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --right, if I really wanted to go. You just--you just--you didn't go just because-- you combined everything together and you just didn't make it very often.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So how often would you go to Jacksonville?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: I don't even remember how--of course, I wasn't but eighteen years old and that was, you know, back--but I don't, I don't know. I don't remember how often we went but I very well remember coasting down the hill and--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What other kinds of hardships did you have beside the fact you couldn't get around?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well as I say, we just come out of--had a depression. I don't know that it was such a hardship. There was a lot more money. You just couldn't buy anything with it.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So in a way the war didn't put a lot--make a lot of difficulties for you?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What positive--what --you already talked about one positive result was the fact that you had more money.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What other positive results do you think were from the war?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, I don't know. I know I was sure glad when it was over.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Because why were you glad when it--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Because I had a husband. I didn't have to--after he got--because he was--they say he discharged in--from Long View. They transferred him to Long View and--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: For all the times he was sick--recovering from his back injury--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --he was still in the service?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: He was still in the service, yeah, because they operated on his back in Walter Reed's Hospital. And--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So he really--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --he really--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --was discharged before the war was over?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No he was--it was--I can't even remember what year the war was over, but I think he was discharged in May, I don't if it was '44--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: The war, I think was over in '45.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, I think that--I think that he was discharged in '44, I believe, because they had transferred him to--down to Long View and--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Okay, let's talk a little bit about your son who was in Vietnam. Tell who he is and what branch of service he was in.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Okay, he was Larry Gill and he was in the Navy. He finished high school in '66 and--and went first semester to T.J.C and then joined the Navy. He said couldn't --didn't believe he could be a foot soldier so--and he was afraid they would draft him and that's why he--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So that was in '67 or early '69.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. Somewhere along there. Seemed like when he joined the Navy, it was such a shock cause he did it while he--at school. And it was such a shock when he come home and told me he that he had joined the Navy. But seems--but it was on this where you joined and you didn't go until--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: A little bit later.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --a little bit later.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --be delayed?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So how did you feel whenever he told you he was going--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Oh, I had felt awful because I didn't--I really didn't think about it. I thought I had him in school. But he went on and joined the Navy anyway.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well you felt awful because you didn't want him to serve or because he hadn't told you --

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I just didn't--I wanted him to finish school the first.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: But they don't always do what you want them to.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So it was a while though before he did actually go?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well it wasn't--well it was a while but it wasn't that long.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And where did he do his basic training?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: In Florida, I believe, is where he was. Seem like he was--I know he was in Florida.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well there's--I think two or three Air Force Bases in--No, he was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: He was in the Navy but I think that's where he was so that he did--he may have done it at San Diego.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And he was in, you told me, in some kind of surveillance?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yeah, he was one of the crew on the surveillance plane that, I don't remember what kind of that plane it was but it flew right above the water tracing submarines.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And you said he was stationed?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well he was stationed all over but he was stationed at Da Nang. That wasn't--at one time and then I kind of think he was in Hawaii when he--when he was discharged. But I don't remember what year he was discharged because he married in '69 but I know he still had to go back before --I mean when he was--he wasn't discharged, he married before. His wife was a school teacher and don't seem like he had to stay that--that long after they married but I don't--because he was here when my daughter married and she married in '71.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: He couldn't tell you too much about what he was doing?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: He didn't. No. He couldn't. He couldn't tell you what--what was going on and when he got back he didn't want to talk about it.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So you really never knew--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I never knew much about what, you know, what he did.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: You knew probably more out of papers, then?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, I'd read the papers but, of course, he never would tell anything that went on. He couldn't afford to tell what, you know, what they were doing, he said, you know.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: How did you feel about that war?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, I take the Fifth Amend--don't--I don't think that we should have ever been in that war, is the way I feel about it.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: How did your feeling compare with the way you felt about World War II?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, we didn't have any choice but to fight in World War II but--but I just didn't think we should have been Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What was the difference in the way people felt and their spirits in those two wars? Did you notice any differences--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No, I don't--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --with people around here talked about the situations?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No. I was never--I had never been a gossip, so I don't--I don't --I really don't know what, you know, what they--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well, what I was thinking about is that World War II, there seemed to be a lot of patriotic spirit.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Do you remember the victory bonds?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Do you remember buying any victory stamps or--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yes, we did. We had, but I can't remember what. I don't remember --I was thinking they were bonds though that we had--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: You bought some war bonds?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: War bonds. Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively)

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well I remember as a little girl in school--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: That we could buy stamps.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Stamps. Uh huh, right.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And you put them in a book.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: And when you got enough you could trade them--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --into a bond, right?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --for a bond. But I think that--that--I know we had several bonds, but I don't--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What about victory gardens during World War II? Do you remember anything about that?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: I stayed with my mother and they live at Summerfield. She always had a garden no matter what but they --we didn't call it a victory garden, it was just mother's garden.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: You remember though about hearing about victory garden?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yeah. I remember it being --

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Those are the two things I really remember was victory --bonds--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Victory--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --and victory garden. Well this has been very interesting to learn about your memories of both wars--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: My memories are not well but--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: --of both those wars, I think that your memory of War World II seems to be more positive than your memory of Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Right. When your child goes, it's different. Well of course, I didn't want my husband going either but you didn't--we had to fight then. I mean, it was--or I felt like we did but anyway--but I didn't, I really didn't think Vietnam should have ever--we should have ever had Vietnam. I think that was political.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Did you worry a lot about your son?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Yeah, sure.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Not knowing--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Didn't know--didn't know what was going on and he couldn't tell you anything.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: What was his attitude like?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well I guess it was okay. He never said anything about, you know, when he came home, we just acted like the war never--there wasn't a war going on. We just--you know we was just glad he was home. But--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: And when he came back he didn't want to talk about it?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: He wouldn't talk about it--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: He didn't have any injury or any kind of difficulties--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: No. No, he never--he didn't--I can't think of any. He was in that--they called him while back, that he had that operation--was it Operation Orange or--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Agent Orange.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Agent Orange and they called him and he had to go to be examined.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: To see if there was any evidence--

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Well, uh huh (Answered affirmatively).

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: How long along ago was that?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: It hadn't been long because--because they found out he was a diabetic whenever--but I can't think, but it has been less than a year.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Now he developed diabetes after the war?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: Uh huh. (Answered affirmatively) He was --they told him when they had sent after he had gone and--this--to be examined. They called him to come in to be examined to see if he had any problems with this Agent Orange and--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Did they find any evidence to that?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: If they did, he didn't tell it because I --he just--he goes--I go to the same--we go to the same doctor. And of course, the doctor knew that I had-- that I was a diabetic and-- And of course, the doctor knew that I was a diabetic and--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: So that's in the family?

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: --so it's in the--I go to his doctor over at Carthage. They live at Beckville and so I had always gone over there to him but he knew that I was a diabetic.

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well I certainly thank you for the interview. Well it's been interesting to me to talk to you and to learn what you remember of the two situations.

sp.speaker: Ahnolia Gill
sp.p: If I wasn't so old, I could remember--

sp.speaker: Jane Purtle
sp.p: Well you remember as well as I do. My mother does remember better than I do. One of the reasons I remembered about victory bonds and everything, she tells me. Talking about the stamps and stuff.
